old:
For a frail older person taking insulin or a gliclazide-type tablet, a low HbA1c can be a sign of more treatment than they need.

HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar over recent months. A low result looks like success. What it doesn't show is whether low blood sugars are happening. In a small US study of 40 older people (37 on insulin) whose HbA1c was 8% or more, 26 had low glucose readings (below 70 mg/dL) over 3 days of continuous monitoring, and 93 in 100 of the 102 low episodes were missed by finger-prick tests and symptoms.

How common is a low HbA1c on these drugs? In 16 Norfolk GP practices, about 3 in 10 people aged 70 or over with type 2 diabetes taking gliclazide-type tablets or insulin had an HbA1c below 53 mmol/mol, and about 1 in 8 were below 48. It was just as common in people with kidney disease or dementia, who are more prone to low sugars. In US national data from 2001 to 2010, 56 in 100 older people with diabetes and very poor health had an HbA1c below 7% (53 mmol/mol). In relatively healthy older people with diabetes it was 63 in 100. Very poor health meant difficulty with two or more everyday activities, or being on dialysis. Of those in very poor health with an HbA1c below 7%, 6 in 10 were on insulin or a sulfonylurea. Neither study measured low sugars directly.

Why it counts: in studies of older people treated for diabetes, those with episodes of low blood sugar were more likely to have falls and fractures. That is a link, not proof of cause.

The other side: across 15 trials and observational studies in people aged 60 or over or frail, tight control was linked with fewer blood vessel complications, but more than twice the rate of severe low sugars, and no clear difference in deaths.

A UK consensus statement says the usual targets of 53 to 59 mmol/mol are too tight for people living with frailty. A deprescribing guideline recommends reducing drugs that cause low sugars in older people at risk.

The question for the next review: have there been any low sugars, and is this dose still needed? Doses are for the diabetes team or GP to change, not for you to change alone.
